Italian regulators said a feature specific to the Facebook app on Android phones could have impacted as many as 20 million people in Italy. [File: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.
The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Meta’s AI age-check goes global: Can it protect teens?list 2 of 3US nonprofits sue tech giants to halt AI developmentlist 3 of 3When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies?end of list
The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.
This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.
Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.
The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.
Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.
The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.

This artist's concept depicts NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft entering interstellar space [NASA/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and ReutersPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.
On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3NASA launches $4.3bn Roman Telescope to uncover universe’s hidden secretslist 2 of 3SpaceX’s showpiece Starship rocket reaches orbit for first timelist 3 of 3Which countries have sent people to space?end of list
The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.
NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.
Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.
Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.
Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.
In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.

Ron Wells and Melanie Joly after Stelco announced it would recall 175 laid off workers in Hamilton, Ontario, November 13, 2026 [Carlos Osorio/Reuters]By Tamara KhandakerPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
Canadian steelmaker Stelco says it will recall all 175 workers laid off at its plant in Hamilton and pay them retroactively, following a weeks-long standoff that pitted workers and the Canadian government against its owner in the United States.
The announcement on Friday came shortly after Canada’s Industry Minister Melanie Joly said she would seek a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Stelco unless she heard from management by the end of the day.

The company said in a statement on Friday that it had reached agreements with enough customers to restart its finishing operations and that workers would be recalled on December 1. They would receive back pay for the standard wages they would have earned while laid off.
The president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, Ron Wells, welcomed the announcement and credited pressure from workers, the union and the government.
At a news conference, he called the layoffs “illegal” and “immoral” which should never have happened.
Alongside him was Joly, who said the outcome sent a message to investors that Canada was “a country of the rule of law and that the law applies to everyone, notwithstanding the size of your wallet.”
“This fight was absolutely worth it,” she said.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, right, speaks as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, left, listens during a news conference in Washington, DC [File: Mariam Zuhaib/AP Photo]By Evan SemonesPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
Over a week after Democrats rode a historic wave of support to retake the United States Congress, divisions within the party seem to be threatening to undermine its newfound political momentum.
Despite growing calls for a change in Congressional leadership, Democrats Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries appear likely to remain at the helm of their respective US Senate and House caucuses.

After amassing the most Democratic power in Washington since 2009, the two New Yorkers are seeking to retain their leadership positions as their party prepares to take control of both chambers in January.
Schumer, the US Senate’s 75-year-old minority leader, is vying to lead Democrats’ new majority in the chamber, a post he previously held during Joe Biden’s presidency. On the other side of the US Capitol, the 56-year-old Jeffries, as the current minority leader in the US House, is seeking the top role of speaker, placing him second in the line of succession for the US presidency.
But the prospect of keeping Schumer and Jeffries in charge has frustrated some Democrats, exposing long-running tensions between Democratic lawmakers who want to maintain continuity and those who believe their midterm victories offer an opportunity to fundamentally reshape the party...

Questions are swirling over Nvidia's future after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO [File: Jonathan Brady/AP Photo]By Andy HirschfeldPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
In the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia, the company has brought in a new interim chief, Colette Kress, who has been with the company since 2013.
Along with Kress, the AI bellwether appointed its first-ever board chair, Harvey Jones, a venture investor with three decades of tech industry experience.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Why did Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resign, and who is Colette Kress?list 2 of 3Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?list 3 of 3Microsoft says affected services fully recovered following worldwide outageend of list
The changes mark a major overhaul of Nvidia’s corporate structure and leadership, which Huang has dominated since cofounding the AI chipmaker in 1993. A powerful figure in Silicon Valley, he stepped down on Thursday following reports of his affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and two employees that have drawn scrutiny from United States lawmakers, the company’s board and shareholders.
Despite the shakeup, the question remains how much of Nvidia’s nearly $4 trillion value was pegged to its longtime leader, who is synonymous with the company’s exponential growth. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, predicted that Nvidia’s value could decline 25 to 30 percent without Huang at the helm.
Historically, executives across corporate America have been beholden to shareholders, who hold executives accountable. In Silicon Valley, however, companies have often been built around a founder’s vision – as was the case for Nvidia.

item.title: Young musicians connect a community across the Line of Control
item.description:
Young musicians connect a community across the Line of Control
Sharing Shina songs online, musicians in Kashmir, Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan are keeping their language alive and renewing ties across the divide.An illustration depicting a divided community connected by music, with a map of India and Pakistan in the background [Jawahir al-Naimi/Al Jazeera]An illustration depicting a divided community connected by music, with a map of India and Pakistan in the background [Jawahir al-Naimi/Al Jazeera]By Ishtayaq RasoolPublished On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026

This feature is part of a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.
In the remote Tulail Valley close to the Line of Control in Indian-administered Kashmir, 25-year-old singer Aasim Yaseen was walking through his village, Buglinder, when a college student from a neighbouring hamlet stopped him.
The young man, Tanveer, took out his phone and played Sangh Mukh Shamah, a song Yaseen had recently released in Shina, their shared language.
The encounter motivated Yaseen.
“People here don’t consider music work,” he says.
“Sometimes I think about going into another profession, but then someone plays my song on their phone, and I keep going.”
Across Gurez in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, Drass in Indian-administered Ladakh, and Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, young musicians like Yaseen are sharing Shina songs on social media. They are helping keep their language alive and renewing ties within a community that has been divided for generations.
The songs cross the Line of Control, which divides Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Kashmir. But the musicians face financial pressures, unreliable internet connections...
